solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Say what would hold a big jug for securing one's breakfast?

blocks.note: e.g. means 'for example', what you write before saying one

blocks.clueFragment: what would hold a big jug
blocks.note: jugs is slang for breasts, and a G is a large bra-cup size

explanation.surface: A leering question about lingerie dressed up as a query about breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: Jugs is crude slang for breasts; bra cups run from A upwards, and G is a big one.
explanation.definitionFit: The china holder keeps a boiled egg upright on the breakfast table, so the egg is held firm while eaten.

clue.text: Celebs refuse to be entertained by a git cavorting

indicators.note: something entertained is taken in as a guest, so one word sits inside another
cavorting is prancing about wildly, so these letters jump into a new order

blocks.note: the four letters rearranged and split around the other word
refuse in the sense of rubbish

explanation.surface: Famous people decline to be amused by some idiot showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb meaning decline; it is the noun, rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The glitterati are the fashionable famous set, a jokey blend of glitter and literati, i.e. celebrities.

clue.text: Hang on – clearing organ out

indicators.note: out means taken away, so the named body part is removed from the longer word

blocks.note: taken as written
the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a pause while an organ is cleared out, as a church or a surgeon might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests a church instrument; it is the ear, removed from CLEARING to leave CLING.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling is to grip tightly and refuse to let go, the same as hanging on.

clue.text: Puff about to get on US beauty contest?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the outside of the other

blocks.note: to puff is to breathe hard
to get on in years is to age

explanation.surface: Someone smoking or panting about getting on stage at an American beauty contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call a beauty contest a pageant, as in Miss America; the question mark flags the regional usage.

clue.text: Certainly time to get fat rugby player's body back inside

indicators.note: back means turned backwards, so the letters read from the end
inside means placed within, so the reversed piece sits in the other word

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
obese means very fat
RU is Rugby Union, the governing body a rugby player belongs to

explanation.surface: It is surely time for a fat rugby player to get his body back on the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' here is an organisation: the Rugby Union, abbreviated RU.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sure is a stock (stage-Irish) phrase for certainly or of course.

clue.text: Reportedly pull article on 'social' dose of cocaine to comply with political leader's decree?

indicators.note: reportedly means as said by others, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: to tow is to pull
the definite article
a social is a party
a line is a single snorted dose of cocaine

explanation.surface: Rumoured drug-taking at a party, mixed into a story about political obedience.
explanation.definitionFit: To toe the party line is an idiom for obeying the official policy laid down by party leaders.

clue.text: Naff spin user's nightmare?

blocks.note: naff is British slang for tasteless or poor
a spin is a short trip out

explanation.surface: A dull spin doctor's account of a nightmare, or a poor drive out.
explanation.walkthrough: Naff is British slang for cheap, tacky or bad.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug user's frightening hallucinogenic experience is called a bad trip, so it is the user's nightmare.

clue.text: Plot involving Sun and Cameron & Co's way of doing things

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for sun (and Sunday)
David Cameron led the Conservatives, or Tories
a line is a policy or approach

explanation.surface: A conspiracy involving the Sun newspaper and David Cameron's methods.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid, but here it is just S; Cameron & Co are the Tories, the Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyline is the sequence of events in a narrative, which is what a plot is.

clue.text: Regulation, markedly stiff length?

blocks.note: first meaning: a law or principle to obey
second meaning: a rigid strip with measurements marked on it

explanation.surface: A regulation about a notably stiff length, with an obvious smutty undertone.
explanation.walkthrough: A carpenter's or folding rule is a stiff measuring strip marked off in units, hence 'markedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rule means both a regulation and a straight measuring stick with markings, like a ruler.

clue.text: One sort of sex education person who's generous

blocks.note: a giving person is generous
the head teacher of a school

explanation.surface: A generous school head offering a particular kind of sex education.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex education' looks like a single phrase, but the definition stops at 'sex'.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving head is slang for performing oral sex, which is one kind of sexual act.

clue.text: Duck getting leg over, look

indicators.note: over suggests a letter rolling over from the end to the front of the word

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O
the last letter is brought round to the start

explanation.surface: Someone ducks while 'getting their leg over' (having sex) and takes a look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's leg over' is British slang for having sex. A duck is zero in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to look at someone lecherously, a leering sort of look.

clue.text: Bastards turning on the old lady – disgrace!

indicators.note: turning means facing about, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: git is British slang for a nasty person
one's old lady is one's mother, Ma

explanation.surface: Outrage at louts turning on an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Git is British slang for an unpleasant person.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of shame or disgrace attached to someone.

clue.text: Ready for it? Like the devil!

blocks.note: first meaning: sexually aroused
second meaning: having horns, as Satan is pictured

explanation.walkthrough: 'Like the devil!' reads as an emphatic 'very much', but it describes the horned devil.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for aroused and literally means having horns, which the devil traditionally does.

clue.text: "Poor sod in hell: Darling's end" is not quite the language of Shakespeare!

definitions.text: not quite the language of Shakespeare!
definitions.note: Old English predates Shakespeare's Early Modern English, hence 'not quite'

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so these letters are knocked into another order
end points to the final letter of the name before it

blocks.note: taken as written
Alistair Darling, Labour Chancellor; his last letter

explanation.surface: A mock quotation about a damned soul and a Chancellor's fate, then a jibe about Shakespearean English.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare wrote Early Modern English; Old English is the much older Anglo-Saxon tongue, which is why the clue says 'not quite'.
explanation.definitionFit: People often wrongly call Shakespeare's language Old English; it is close in name but centuries off, hence the hedge.

clue.text: New PM, real turd, ditching Right and Left as a figment of imagination

definitions.note: a phrase describing how something came about, i.e. invented

indicators.note: ditching means throwing away, so two letters are dropped
new means made fresh, so the letters are formed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
R for right; one is removed
L for left; removed

explanation.surface: A satirical swipe: a new Prime Minister is a real turd who abandons both right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dreamt up is invented, existing only in the mind like a figment of imagination.

clue.text: This should interrupt the smooth ride of broadcast by Nick

definitions.text: This should interrupt the smooth ride

blocks.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
to nick is to steal, as is to pocket

explanation.surface: A TV programme by someone called Nick disrupts an otherwise smooth run.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick is British slang for steal; 'broadcast' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An air pocket is a region of turbulent air that makes an aircraft drop suddenly, jolting a smooth flight.

clue.text: Perform sexual act at the rear in Strand, with decorum

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

blocks.note: a ply is a strand of yarn or rope

blocks.clueFragment: Perform sexual act at the rear
blocks.note: slang for anal licking

explanation.surface: A lewd act performed round the back in the Strand, a London street, yet done with decorum.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a London street, but here strand means a single thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Primly means in a proper, prudish way, i.e. with decorum.

clue.text: Labour's origin: true spin, finding a place in Bush's heart

indicators.note: spin means whirl round, so these letters get shuffled into a new order
the heart of a word is its central letters
finding a place in means settling inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the central pair of letters of the name
rearranged

explanation.surface: Political spin: Labour Party origins finding favour with George W Bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British party; it is childbirth, which begins in the womb. The wordplay also hints at Bush's heart being the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour, the birth process, begins in the womb, the organ where a baby grows.

clue.text: Leader of Senate has dead crude way – most blue

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
crude means unrefined, so the letters are put in a raw new order

blocks.note: first letter
rearranged
St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: The Senate leader has a dead, crude manner and is the most obscene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' suggests rude, which suits the surface, but here it means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means unhappy, so most blue is the superlative of sad.

clue.text: Gut reactions of former Home Secretary bagging contract

indicators.note: bagging means capturing and holding, so one word surrounds the other

blocks.note: Merlyn Rees was Labour Home Secretary in the late 1970s
to flex a muscle is to contract it

explanation.surface: An ex-minister landing a contract provokes instinctive reactions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a business deal; it is the verb for tightening a muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: Reflexes are automatic responses, the involuntary reactions people call gut reactions.

clue.text: It's a weakness of Cook, welcoming trouble (doorstepper at heart)

indicators.note: welcoming means letting in, so the other pieces go inside the outer word
at heart points to the single central letter of the word

blocks.note: to fry is to cook
to ail is to trouble
the sixth of eleven letters

explanation.surface: A politician named Cook has a soft spot for awkward doorstepping reporters.
explanation.walkthrough: A doorstepper is a journalist who waits at someone's front door for a comment.
explanation.definitionFit: Frailty is weakness of body or character, so a frailty is a weakness.

clue.text: Thus could Anglia TV be taken to be a git

definitions.text: Thus could Anglia TV be taken to be a git

blocks.clueFragment: Thus could Anglia TV be taken to be a git
blocks.note: surface reading: someone sneering at a regional TV station
setter's reading: take the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of this name and you spell 'a git'

explanation.surface: A jibe that Anglia, an English regional ITV channel, is idiotic.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the alternate letters of ANGLIATV from the start: A, G, I, T. The answer is the adverb telling you which letters to take.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes taking letters in odd-numbered places, and also means strangely, as the jibe is.

clue.text: "Member covered in piss" claim

indicators.note: covered in means surrounded by, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: piss is British slang for weak beer
a limb, one of the body's members

explanation.surface: A tabloid claim that someone's member was found soaked in urine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' hints at the penis; it is a leg. In British slang piss also means beer.
explanation.definitionFit: To allege is to claim something without yet proving it.

clue.text: Camilla just started into strip, bar entrance!

definitions.note: noun phrase: a bar for an entrance

indicators.note: just started means only the opening letter is used
into places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: a lath is a thin strip of wood
first letter

explanation.surface: Camilla, Queen Consort, had barely begun to strip when told she was barred from entering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip' looks like undressing, but it is a thin strip of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A latch is the simple bar that holds a door or gate shut, a bar on an entrance.

clue.text: Bollocks turn over – give it a rest!

blocks.note: TO is the abbreviation printed at a page foot, as in PTO
the call for quiet

explanation.surface: An exasperated 'bollocks, roll over and shut up!'
explanation.walkthrough: Bollocks is British slang for nonsense as well as testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosh is British slang for nonsense, the same meaning as the exclamation bollocks.

clue.text: Starts to suck off actor knight in boozer

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their opening letters

blocks.note: the opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A lewd scene involving a knighted actor in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, which suits the surface, but here it means a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A soak is a habitual heavy drinker, which is another meaning of boozer.

clue.text: About G-spot: it lies pointlessly somewhere behind the tongue

indicators.note: pointless means without a compass point, so one such letter is dropped
about means moving around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
loses the S, which is south

explanation.surface: A sex-ed jibe that the G-spot claim is a pointless lie somewhere behind the tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: S for south is a compass point; removing it from 'lies' is the pointless part.
explanation.definitionFit: The epiglottis is the flap of cartilage at the root of the tongue, lying behind it in the throat.

clue.text: Washed out truss donned for a formal occasion?

blocks.note: pale, drained of colour
to truss is to tie up

explanation.surface: A faded surgical truss worn to a smart do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Truss' suggests a hernia support; it means bind.
explanation.definitionFit: White tie is the most formal dress code, a white bow tie and tailcoat worn at grand events.

clue.text: Ejaculation that boosted an old sailor on the pull

definitions.text: Ejaculation that boosted an old sailor on the pull

blocks.clueFragment: Ejaculation that boosted an old sailor on the pull
blocks.note: surface reading: a randy seaman's climax while trying to pick someone up
setter's reading: a cry that helped sailors heave together on a rope

explanation.walkthrough: Ejaculation is an old word for an exclamation, and 'on the pull' means hauling a rope, not seeking a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the traditional sea-shanty cry, an exclamation sailors chanted to keep time while hauling.
